q: A terraced amphitheatre above the town of Ampuis takes its name from the way the sun bakes it. Which appellation?
exp: The roasted slope, and the northernmost of the valley's crus. Its terraces are held up by dry stone walls that need constant rebuilding after heavy rain.

q: Growers around Angers speak of Anjou noir and Anjou blanc. What does that pair of names distinguish?
opts: Dark schist to the west against pale tuffeau limestone to the east
Red wine production to the west against white wine production to the east
exp: The colours are the rocks, not the wine. The black schist belongs to the old Armorican massif and gives the brooding dry Chenin and sweet Layon wines; the white limestone further east gives the softer, chalkier style around Saumur.

q: Italy's peninsula is divided lengthwise by which mountain range?
exp: The Apennines run the length of the country from Liguria down to Calabria, while the Alps close off the north. Their altitude is what keeps nights cool even in the far south.

q: Roast pork with crackling arrives with a spoonful of apple sauce on the side. Which pour handles the fat and the sweet sauce at once?
opts: A soft, low-acid white with no sugar
exp: The apple sauce is the complication rather than the pork: a bone-dry wine tastes stripped beside it, so a little sugar in the glass keeps the wine's own fruit intact while the acidity deals with the crackling. A dessert wine overshoots so far that the meat stops registering at all.

q: The bottler's address on a French label names a town in a department far from the appellation printed above it. What does that address actually tell you?
opts: That the wine was declassified before bottling
That the appellation claim has been made in error and the bottle should not have been sold
Where the bottling was carried out
That the wine was made from bought-in grapes
exp: The bottler statement identifies a business and its premises for traceability, while origin is carried entirely by the appellation. The two lines can point at different places with nothing at all wrong, which is why an address is a poor guide to where a wine comes from.

q: Rather than bottle its parcels separately, one family that has farmed the hill of Hermitage since the fifteenth century assembles fruit from right across it into a single red each year. Which domaine?
exp: The blend draws on Les Bessards, Le Meal, L'Hermite and other named sectors of the slope, and putting them together is treated as the whole art of the appellation, because each supplies something the others cannot. The negociant houses of the hill assemble across the slope as well, but none of them can show vines held by one family for five centuries.

q: Granite at seven hundred metres, in the coolest corner of a famously hot region, marks which Alentejo sub-region?
exp: Portalegre sits in the Serra de Sao Mamede against the Spanish border, high enough for fresher acidity and a later picking date than the plains allow. Granja-Amareleja, by contrast, is among the hottest ground in Portugal.

q: A label reading simply Bordeaux AOC tells you what about sourcing?
opts: The fruit is from the Medoc
exp: It is the regional catch-all, and the majority of Bordeaux by volume is sold under it. Nothing about a commune or a rank is implied.

q: Botrytis never appears in a warm dry German autumn, yet a Beerenauslese is still declared. How?
opts: The fruit was frozen in the winery before it was pressed
The berries raisined on the vine with no fungus
The must was concentrated by boiling it down before fermentation
Sussreserve was blended in later to lift the sugar
exp: The Pradikat is a sugar threshold read on the must at harvest, and shrivelling in dry heat is another way to cross it. Sussreserve sweetens a finished wine but cannot lift that reading, and neither a freezer in the winery nor a must boiled down before fermentation may be used to reach one: Eiswein is the single frozen-fruit Pradikat, and it requires the freeze to happen out on the vine. Wines made this way taste pure and grapey where a botrytised version would be honeyed and savoury.

q: Barnyard, sticking plaster and leather notes are usually attributed to what?
exp: A spoilage yeast. Opinion divides on trace levels, and at higher levels it flattens fruit and homogenises a range.

q: Two related whites grown side by side in the Pyrenean foothills are separated on their labels by the words Petit and Gros, and a guest reads that pair as a ranking. What do the two words record?
opts: The relative standing of the two wines, smaller meaning lesser
The order in which the two are picked
The age of the vines the fruit came from
The size of the berry, nothing more
exp: Small berries carry more skin against less juice, so the smaller-berried of the pair gives the more concentrated wine and has the greater reputation, in dry wines and sweet ones alike. Size and quality line up here by an accident of botany rather than because the words mean anything of the sort. The same pair of words elsewhere separates two entirely unrelated varieties, so it is never a rank.

q: A group of Clare Valley producers agreed in 2000 to bottle their Riesling under a closure Australian wineries had tried in the 1970s and abandoned. What were they trying to stop?
opts: Cork taint and the bottle-to-bottle variation
Sediment forming in the bottle during long ageing
The wine losing colour under shop lighting
Sulphur dioxide escaping through the closure
exp: A taut dry Riesling exposes a tainted or prematurely oxidised bottle more brutally than almost any other wine, and the Clare growers were losing bottles at random. Australian trials in the 1970s had already put premium Riesling under screwcap and been dropped when buyers balked, so this was a revival rather than a first. It stuck: the screwcap now seals most Australian wine at every price, and the argument has moved on to how much oxygen a liner should admit.
